Post defends Bantu Somalis and calls out the original poster as a 'stupid racist idoor' (Isaaq clan slur) — this is counter-speech defending Bantu Somalis against racism, though 'idoor' is itself a clan slur directed at the interlocutor.

Post mocks an 'idoor' (Isaaq clan slur) user by claiming their clan has always been led by Ethiopians, using a historically loaded clan insult to demean lineage legitimacy — clan-based insult targeting Isaaq.

'Faqash' (derogatory term for Siad Barre regime loyalists/Darod clan militias) is used to accuse an opponent of intellectual dishonesty and historical revisionism against the Isaaq — the slur is wielded as a political-clan insult.

'Faqash' (Barre-regime/Darod clan slur) is deployed, and then 'Somali' identity itself is equated to AIDS as a disease metaphor — dehumanising Somalia-identifying people and implying Somalilanders will purge this identity, constituting an exclusion demand with dehumanising language.

terms: Burn it all to the ground
exp: Post calls Kenya a 'failed neo-colonial experiment' and uses the metaphor 'burn it all to the ground' in the context of anti-government protest hashtags — political hyperbole and anti-government dissent rather than identity-based hate speech.

Post dehumanises South Sudanese people by describing them as an inherently violent population that should be left to die rather than 'fed' and allowed to 'breed' — using animal-husbandry language that strips humanity and implies a genocidal exclusion/elimination logic.

References the mass killing and displacement of Sudanese people and suggests passively allowing ongoing violence to continue ('let nature take its course'), which functions as an existential-threat marker by implying the killing of a group should proceed unchecked, though it stops short of explicit incitement.
A political/historical argument defending Somaliland's sovereignty claim against Djibouti's recognition dispute — no hate speech, slurs, or identity-based attack present.

The hashtag '#takfiri' (one who declares others apostates/infidels) is used alongside a video clip tag, functioning as a religious slur/label, though the post is largely a hashtag dump and context is unclear.
A factual historical account of Rwandan genocide atrocities against Tutsi at Munini in 1994 — this is documentation/counter-speech, not hate speech.

Swahili post telling 'Mount Kenya' voters (a coded reference to the Kikuyu/Central Kenya ethnic bloc who supported Ruto) to stop complaining, combining regional-ethnic targeting with political criticism of President Ruto.
Abusive profanity directed at the Kenya National Highways Authority (@KeNHAKenya) over road infrastructure — no identity-based hate, but contains abusive language targeting a named institution.

Dehumanises Foreign Affairs CS Mudavadi by calling him a 'fat orangutan' (primate dehumanisation) and tags his ethnic origin (Vihiga/Luhya), while criticising government inaction on Kenyan drivers killed abroad.
Swahili post calling Kenya's leaders 'ngurue' (pigs/swine) — derogatory animal insult directed at political leaders generally rather than a specific ethnic/identity group.

Frames DRC and South Sudanese nationals collectively as responsible for killing Kenyan drivers abroad while living 'like kings' in Kenya — an accusation-mirror framing that casts a national/foreign group as both aggressors and undeserving beneficiaries.
Criticises President Ruto using 'Sugoi conmanship' (referencing his hometown Sugoi as a stand-in for personal dishonesty) — primarily political attack on an individual, borderline questionable.
Calls for the hanging of those allied with 'thieves and corrupt people' (wezi na wafisadi) — an explicit incitement to lethal violence against a broadly defined political category of persons.

Uses the slur 'Faqash' (pejorative for Siad Barre's regime/Darод loyalists) and 'kacaan' (socialist revolution era) to delegitimise Mogadishu/federal Somalia by comparing it unfavourably to Somaliland in a political dispute.
Somali-language post celebrating Somaliland's international recognition after alleged attempts to destabilise it — a political statement with no hate speech or slurs.
Calls an unnamed individual 'nacas' (fool/idiot) and 'xoolo' (livestock/animal) — a dehumanising animal slur applied to a specific person in a Somali TikTok context.

Frames Sudan's civil war as Arab Sudanese ethnically targeting Black African Sudanese (150,000 killed), with UAE funding — uses 'unalived' as a euphemism for mass killing; functions as dangerous speech highlighting existential ethnic threat, though framed as reporting/advocacy.
Uses 'laan gaab' (short lineage — a slur for minority/low-status clans) to insult a named individual (Firdhiye/Jaamac Siyaad), framing him as lacking proper clan credentials.
Abusive accusation directed at Kenya National Police Service (@NPSOfficial_KE) alleging corruption, rape of minors and killing of youth — targeted institutional abuse with no identity-based hate.

Argues Kenya made a mistake expelling white settlers and calls Mau Mau independence fighters 'frauds' — dismisses anti-colonial struggle with an ethnic/political slur, but primarily a provocative political opinion.

Duplicate of post 4 — Swahili text telling 'Mount Kenya' voters (Kikuyu ethnic bloc) to stop complaining about Ruto while also calling for Ruto's removal; political criticism with ethnic regional coding.
Political criticism blaming Uhuru Kenyatta's 2013 election for Kenya's current problems — standard partisan political opinion with no hate speech or identity attack.
Singles out Kikuyu people ('Wakikuyu') as collectively engaging in a charity-fraud scheme — ethnic stereotyping combined with a specific accusation against an unnamed Kikuyu individual.

Challenges Somali historical claims in East Africa by citing the slur 'Jareer' (hard-hair, anti-Bantu racial slur) as evidence of Somali contempt for Bantu rulers — the term is quoted critically/descriptively to argue against Somali supremacist narratives, making this counter-speech rather than hate speech.

Uses 'jareer' (anti-Bantu slur) and 'adoon' (slave — derogatory term for low-status/Bantu Somalis) self-deprecatingly while commenting on Somali women's attractiveness — casual use of ethnic/caste slurs normalises derogatory language even if humorous intent is implied.
Blanket dismissal of Somalis as lacking political philosophers — a derogatory national/ethnic stereotype, though without explicit slur terms.

Challenges the interlocutor to name a Somali political philosopher — framed as a debate point that implicitly reinforces a stereotype about Somali intellectual capacity, but could also be read as a genuine rhetorical question.
Post uses ableist slur ('retarded') to collectively demean Somalis as an ethnic group, constituting group-level derogatory abuse.
'Soroob' is a mild dismissive term for hardliners refusing Somaliland recognition; the post is political commentary contrasting Somaliland's stability with Mogadishu's, without identity-based hate.
Post insults Qatar as a 'tiny home of terrorists' feeding jihadists while asserting Somaliland's sovereignty; the 'terrorist' label applied to a nation constitutes group-level insult.
Near-identical to post 2, repeating 'tiny home of terrorists' against Qatar while asserting Somaliland sovereignty — group-level insult against a nation.
Post is political commentary arguing Somaliland's decolonisation pre-dates Djibouti's independence; mildly dismissive of Djibouti ('little city state') but no identity-based hate.

'Faqash' (a derogatory slur for supporters of the Barre regime, often targeting Darood) is used to dismiss opponents as regime collaborators who falsify history, while asserting Somaliland was a protectorate, not colonised.
Post dehumanises Darood and Hawiye clan members as 'apes' and uses the regime-collaborator slur 'faqash', constituting clan-based dehumanisation.
'Idoor' is an anti-Isaaq slur used to dismiss the interlocutor while making territorial claims (Berbera) framed as punishment for Isaaq militia actions.
Post expresses political aspiration for Somali Galbeed (Ogaden) independence from Ethiopia, describing Ethiopia as a 'failed and forced nation'; political criticism without coded slurs.

Post dismisses Mau Mau independence fighters as 'frauds' responsible for Kenya's post-colonial failures while lamenting the departure of white settlers, constituting an insult to a liberation movement with ethnic overtones.

Post criticises the Kenya National Police Service for corruption, sexual abuse and killings of youth; while insulting ('fools'), it targets an institution not an identity group, making it political criticism.

Post attributes post-election violence arson in Nairobi to Mungiki (a Kikuyu-associated criminal/political militia), framing it as ethnic revenge while distinguishing 'locals' — an ethno-political blame attribution.
Post blames Kenya's 63 years of mismanagement on Kikuyu and Kalenjin ethnic groups and calls the country a 'shit hole', constituting ethnic-group-level insult and stereotyping.
Post calls an unnamed individual (contextually a Sudanese political figure) 'evil' and holds him responsible for 175,000 deaths; political condemnation of an individual without coded identity hate.

Referencing a mass atrocity (500,000 killed, 1,000,000 displaced) and saying 'let nature take its course' implicitly endorses continued violence against Sudanese people, meeting the existential-threat and exclusion-demand Benesch markers.
'Dhilo' (whore/prostitute) and 'gaal' (infidel/apostate) are combined to attack a Somali woman who has apparently left Islam, using both gendered and religious slurs to deny her Somali identity.
'Murtad' (apostate) is hurled as an insult at the interlocutor while debating racial dimensions of Arab human trafficking of Somalis; the religious slur is used as a personal attack.
Again uses 'murtad' (apostate) as an insult in a debate about Somali involvement in Libyan human trafficking, targeting the opponent's religious standing as a rhetorical weapon.

Post accuses named Nigerian political figures (Malami, Buhari) of sponsoring jihadists and links their actions to the kidnapping of Nnamdi Kanu; political condemnation of individuals with no identity-group hate — tangentially Kenya-relevant.
Headline compares South Sudanese people to goats ('Like Goats'), a dehumanising animal comparison applied to a civilian population experiencing humanitarian abandonment.
Kikuyu-language post reflects on the Kenyatta era, expresses communal pride in the Kikuyu and references Kibaki; primarily in-group political reminiscence without inter-ethnic hate targeting others.
Post criticises Kenyan politicians broadly for corruption and reducing citizens to beggars; insults are directed at a political class, not an identity group — political criticism.

Post frames a political confrontation as a 'revolution' and warns elites they are fleeing and seeking asylum, suggesting past mistakes (likely referencing protest violence) will not be repeated — an implicit threat of collective action against a political group meeting existential-threat and exclusion-demand markers.
Post labels two named individuals from Kenya and Uganda as foreign destroyers of 'our country' (USA context), using nationalist othering of African-linked figures.

'Wajinga' (idiots/fools), 'jaluo'/'wajaluo' (derogatory for Luo ethnicity), and 'wajaka' (a dismissive slur) collectively dehumanise Luo people as stupid thieves, constituting ethnic dehumanisation and stereotype-based accusation.
Swahili post demanding foreigners produce papers or be expelled ('warudi kwao' = go back to their country) by 2027, with declared intent to keep pushing that agenda.
Swahili post dismissively tolerating foreigners arriving as long as they don't vote, implying they are unwelcome and illegitimate residents.
Post uses 'qaniis' (Somali slur for homosexual) and body-shaming insults to demean a named individual (Warabe), deploying homophobic and gendered ridicule.
Diplomatic commentary sharing Somaliland MFA's response to foreign ministers, dismissing critics as 'failed states' — political criticism without identity-based hate.
Post criticises the OIC and Arab League as irrelevant and labels Somalia's government an 'Islamic Regime' linked to terrorism — political/institutional criticism with mild derogatory framing.

Somali post mocking Dhulbahante clan prisoners in Somaliland jails with sexual innuendo ('dhunkashada' = kissing/following), using clan identity for ridicule while expressing shame about Somali women.
Brief reply rejecting 'Somalis who want to ruin our country' — political exclusionary sentiment but too vague to confirm identity-based hate without more context.
Post uses 'faqash' (slur for Barre-regime loyalists/Darod) to mock political opponents and dismiss the Somali Republic as a 'non-existent entity'.
Arabic post taunting Somaliland MFA account using 'حماراتي' (plural of donkey — dehumanising insult), claiming they were 'trampled' in Yemen.

Swahili post calling Tanzania a 'country of sheep' (makondoo), invoking killings of children, pregnant women and youth, and implying Tanzanians will retaliate on 23rd — dehumanisation combined with an implicit incitement framing.
Swahili post accusing a Kikuyu person of being jealous of Luos — inter-ethnic taunt using ethnic identity labels as the basis for insult.
Post uses 'Mooryaan' (bandit/gangster slur) to dismiss a group as wanting to deprive Somalis of their rights, deploying clan-associated contempt.
Arabic post telling an interlocutor to first 'liberate Sharjah and Ajman' before congratulating Somaliland, using 'الشرذمة' (rabble/riffraff) as a collective insult.
Post attacks a named individual as an 'idoor' (anti-Isaaq clan slur), 'yahuudi' (Jew — used derogatorily), and 'bootlicker', stacking clan and antisemitic slurs to discredit her.
Post correcting a Saudi account's map regarding Somaliland's history — factual/political speech with no identity-based attack.
Post accuses a named woman of hypocrisy and explicitly states 'we don't want idoor (anti-Isaaq clan slur) in our country', constituting an exclusion demand against a clan group.
Post dismisses Somaliland's legitimacy by renaming it 'Isaaqistaan', using the Isaaq clan label as a reductive ethnic slur against the territory.
Post insults Qatar as 'home of terrorist' and accuses it of 'feeding terrorists around the world' — derogatory national/religious labelling used to dismiss Qatar's diplomatic position on Somaliland.

Post implies Somalia's problems are inherent to Somalis themselves (not systems/governance), suggesting importing Norwegians would 'fix' the country — a dehumanising ethnic-determinist trope denying Somali agency.
French-language geopolitical commentary on Morocco's potential recognition of Somaliland — analytical political speech with no identity-based attack.
'Idorow somali yar yar hala dayo' uses 'idoor' (anti-Isaaq clan slur) and 'hala dayo' (let them be killed/let them die) — an explicit incitement to lethal violence against a named clan group.
TikTok post repeatedly deploying 'idoor' (anti-Isaaq clan slur) as a hashtag label for Somaliland-associated content, using clan contempt as framing.

Post uses 'idoor' (anti-Isaaq slur), 'jareer' (anti-Bantu racial slur meaning 'hard hair'), 'dabacayuun' (submissive/sellout slur), and sexualised language ('futada dhiibta' = giving backside) to sexually humiliate and racially degrade named female figure Khadra Jama Omar while mocking recognition of Somaliland.
Post juxtaposes 'Idoor' (anti-Isaaq clan slur) and 'Ogadeen' (Darod sub-clan) in a mocking comparison, using clan labels to stoke inter-clan rivalry.

Post collectively labels Hutus as inherently genocidal racists ('still claiming to kill more if they get into power'), using genocide history to dehumanise an entire ethnicity and imply ongoing existential threat.
Post criticises Kikuyu and Kalenjin-dominated political leadership for mismanaging Kenya, mixing ethnic labelling with political grievance but stopping short of a call to violence.
Post deflects a charge of tribalism onto Mount Kenya-region parties and links them historically to the Mungiki sect, combining political criticism with ethnic attribution.

'Itungati' means Mungiki fighters; the post addresses Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua ('wamunyoro') directly and declares that no more Mount Kenya-east leaders shall ever lead the country again, amounting to an ethnic exclusion demand.
Post makes a comparative political observation about Kikuyu presidents and Mungiki militia patronage; critical commentary on ethnic-political dynamics without a direct hate call.
Post asserts that the Kikuyu president (Kibaki) weaponised Mungiki as a state militia in 2007/8, a contested political-historical claim with ethnic framing.
Post implies that critics of Kibaki's legacy are Kalenjin (those 'named kip'), framing political disagreement along ethnic lines with a light insinuation.
A mocking one-liner dismissing someone's focus on Kikuyu issues as an unhealthy fixation; borderline insult without substantive hate content.
'Murtad' means apostate; the post attacks a Somali woman as a mentally deficient apostate lesbian feminist, stacking religious and gender slurs as personal abuse.

'Jareer' is a racial slur for Bantu/hard-hair Somalis; 'gaal raac' means infidel-followers/pagans; the post denies the target's Somali identity, racially dehumanises them, and brands them historical pagans.
'Dayuus' is a grave Islamic insult for a man with no honour over female kin; 'gaal' means infidel — the post hurls religious slurs at the target to shame him and dismiss his criticism.
'Gaal caabud' means infidel-worshipper; the post dismisses an Arabic-culture defender as an infidel-worshipper while defending Somali cultural practice.
Post is a political statement asserting Somaliland's historical claim to statehood; no hate speech content.

'Soroob' is a Somali term for those who cling to something futile; the post is political commentary contrasting Somaliland's stability with Mogadishu's dependence on foreign protection — no hate speech.
Post criticises a named Somaliland political figure as a blowhard who uses thugs against citizens, including women and youth — political criticism of an individual leader without group-identity hate.
Post applies the 'Somali pirates' stereotype to a person or group in a non-literal derogatory generalisation, invoking a well-known dehumanising ethnic trope.

Post reports on a politically coded operation name — 'Operation Tame the Mountain' — directed at Mount Kenya communities, framing state/political actors as mobilising against an ethnic region; shares without condemnation, amplifying an existential-threat framing.
'Ukabila' means tribalism in Swahili; post criticises President Ruto for spreading tribalism, framing a Linda Mwananchi event in Kisumu as a test — political accountability commentary.
Post critiques systemic political corruption and tribalism going back to colonial times — general political grievance without a specific group identity target.
Post, likely from a US context, labels a Kenyan and Ugandan as foreign destroyers of 'our country' (America), expressing nativist anti-African sentiment.
Brief ambiguous question about withdrawing Kenyans while natives feel insecure — no hate content detectable.
Post uses a 'why do Africans invade Europe' framing to contest African migration rights while minimising European presence in Kenya — nationalist/nativist rhetoric with anti-African undertones.
Post praises security agencies and notes those involved should leave — neutral civic commentary, no hate content.
'Munonga' is an anti-Rwandan/Congolese ethnic slur; the post tells the targeted individual to 'go back to Kenya,' combining a derogatory ethnic label with a xenophobic expulsion taunt.

'Qaniis' is a Somali slur for a gay/effeminate man; 'dl' means down-low (closeted); the post sexually mocks a Somali man with homophobic and body-shaming slurs while telling him to stay away from Somali women.

'SNM' is the Somaliland national movement (Isaaq-linked); 'wiilo' means stray bullets/chaos; 'jamaca siyad' alludes to Siad Barre loyalists; the post derides Somaliland's 34-year state-building as having been destroyed in 22 minutes by four gunmen, mocking its legitimacy as a 'sanbuse state' (pastry/hollow state).
Post calls for the expulsion or imprisonment of all Somalis from the United States, constituting a collective expulsion incitement against a national/ethnic group.

Arabic post accuses a Somaliland MFA supporter of hypocrisy and shamelessness for defending a state they claim southerners (Mogadishu/FGS side) massacred — political criticism with some identity framing but no clear slur or incitement.
Dismisses Somaliland's statehood claim by mockingly renaming it the 'Sambusa State' — political ridicule rather than identity-based hate speech.
Sarcastic joke about people who claim credit for building Somalia, no hate speech content.

Somali post labels Madobe a 'devil' and 'foreign spy' holding intelligence for Kenya on Kismayo, and calls both politicians 'baboons' (boonooyinka) — dehumanising political insult targeting two named figures and the Gedo community's political choices.
Contested political claim that Kenyan independence was a lie — political provocation without identity-based slur or incitement.

Swahili post calls Mt Kenya people 'dogs' (maumbwa) and 'garbage' (takataka), wishes they would be banished to the Chalbi desert to suffer, and tells them to 'kill yourselves' — dehumanisation and lethal incitement targeting the Mt Kenya/Kikuyu ethnic bloc.
Stereotypes Kikuyus as the most tribal ethnic group in Kenya — low-level ethnic insult/stereotype.
Asserts that Kikuyus are the most tribalistic group in Kenya — ethnic stereotype/insult.
Swahili post warns that without liberating the country it will end up like South Sudan or Somalia — political commentary using those states as cautionary examples, no hate speech.

terms: You people need to leave our lands
exp: 'Idoor' is an anti-Isaaq/northern clan slur; the post strips Isaaq people of Somali identity and demands their expulsion from Somali territory to Israel or Socotra — clan-based exclusion demand and identity denial.
Uses the anti-Isaaq slur 'idoor' to deny the target's Somali identity — clan-based insult.
Somali post calls someone a 'fool/idiot' (doqon), uses the anti-Isaaq slur 'idoor', and says they are not Somali — clan-based insult denying identity.
Labels Qatar a 'home of terrorists' in the context of Somaliland recognition politics — political/national insult rather than protected-group hate speech.
Arabic post mockingly laughs at Somaliland's claim to independent statehood — political ridicule without identity-based slur.

'Faqash' is a derogatory slur for former Siad Barre regime loyalists/Darood; the post nostalgically credits pre-faqash era artists (Khadijo Daleys, Nakruma) with transcending clan (qabilkada) — the slur is used pejoratively even if in a music appreciation context.
Historical analytical questions about the Mungiki militia and Kikuyu violence during Kenya's 2007/08 post-election violence — factual inquiry, not hate speech.
Labels Qatar a 'terrorist funding source' to delegitimise its stance on Somaliland — political/national insult without protected-group hate targeting.
Post equates the ethnonym 'Somali' with the word 'Criminal', collectively criminalising the entire Somali ethnic/national group through pseudo-etymological dehumanisation.
Repeats the claim that Qatar is a terrorism sponsor in the context of Somaliland recognition — political insult against a state, not a protected identity group.
Claims Kenya is governed by a western puppet — standard political criticism without identity-based hate speech.

Post uses flooding/invasion framing against Ugandans (and other foreigners) and collectively associates Ugandans with illegal abortion services — xenophobic accusation-mirror stereotype presenting immigrants as a criminal threat.
Swahili post suggests giving citizenship to foreigners (with 'kasongo' used as a dismissive label for Congolese) so they can go stand there — low-level xenophobic dismissal.

Questions whether Kenya should allow foreign nationals who are not investors, listing multiple nationalities — xenophobic framing but expressed as a policy question without explicit slurs or incitement.
Contrasts foreigners in Kenya (deemed illegal) with Kenyans in the diaspora (deemed legal) — xenophobic framing expressed as a factual comparison rather than explicit incitement.
Post frames ghetto residents as non-Kenyan foreigners paid to cause trouble, using the accusation-mirror trope (foreign orchestration) and implying they should be excluded/removed.

This is a conspiracy-theory attack on Barack Obama claiming he was born in Kenya and committed identity fraud — a recycled 'birther' slur targeting an individual rather than a group, political in nature rather than ethnic hate speech.

Post calls for re-registration and deportation of undocumented foreigners in Kenya — framed as policy advocacy rather than explicit identity hate, but othering in tone; borderline political/administrative rather than hate speech.

Post criticises former President Moi for handing out Kenyan passports to 'international miscreants,' blending nationalist grievance with political criticism of leadership — more political critique than identity-based hate.
Post directly insults a Nigerian woman with gendered abuse ('ugly', 'Neanderthal world'), combining national-foreigner contempt with misogynistic personal attack directed at a specific interlocutor.

Somali post expresses distrust of Turkey, describing it as a 'hidden coloniser' of Somalia and saying only southern Somalia can endure it — political/geopolitical opinion rather than group hate speech.

Somali post condemns President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud ('sole dictator, land-grabber of the people') for imprisoning activist Sadiyo Bajaj without food, calling it terrorism and demanding her release — political criticism/counter-speech, not hate speech.

Post uses 'jareer' (anti-Bantu racial slur meaning 'hard hair') as an insult against a non-Somali interlocutor while asserting Somali supremacy over all of East Africa — racial dehumanisation with exclusion/dominance framing.
Post dismisses a Nigerian commentator on Somali affairs using 'Jareer Yahow' — a derogatory racial slur targeting Black Africans of Bantu descent — to exclude him from political discourse.
Post uses 'jareer' (anti-Bantu racial slur) to demean a group and insult the interlocutor's intelligence for sympathising with them.
Post insults a woman for associating with 'ajnebi jareer' (foreign Black/Bantu people), combining racial contempt with gendered slut-shaming.
Somali post supports Somaliland protesters in Berbera (Barbara), criticises misgovernance and a 12-hour power cut as shameful — political criticism of governance with no identity-based hate.

'Qaniis' (homosexual slur), 'danyeer' (monkey/animal dehumanisation), and 'adoon' (slave) are hurled at the former Somaliland president, combining homophobic, dehumanising, and ethnic/political abuse.
Post describes 2007 inter-ethnic tensions but recounts community elders urging restraint against retaliation — this is counter-speech/historical narrative, not hate speech.

Post criticises a group (implied Somali/Muslim residents of Nairobi neighbourhoods like Eastleigh) for neglecting home counties, using 'useless human beings' — derogatory but ambiguous in target; borderline ethnic othering.

'Ngombe' (cattle/dehumanising slur) is used to describe those who guided attackers to non-Kikuyu homes in the 2007 Nyandarua-to-Nakuru violence, implicitly framing the incident as organised ethnic targeting — dehumanisation with accusation-mirror risk marker.
'Idoor' is an anti-Isaaq clan slur; post uses it ('filthy idoor') to dismiss an interlocutor challenging Somali identity claims.
Post repeats the anti-Isaaq clan slur 'Idoor waa idoor' ('Idoor is Idoor') mockingly to dismiss a Somaliland critic.
Post uses 'pathetic idoor' (anti-Isaaq slur) to mock someone's Somali identity and delegitimise Somaliland as a 'clan enclave.'

Post defends Isaaq clan's Somali identity while labelling opponents as spreading a 'faqash/Mooryaan narrative' — using two established clan-political slurs (pro-Barre regime loyalists; bandits) to discredit adversaries.

Arabic post references the Isaaq clan and their 'genocide' ('إبادتهم'), using an accusation-mirror framing ('your scheme returned to your throats') and mocking 35 years of failure to 'agree' — invokes the historical genocide as a threat reminder, constituting dangerous speech.
'Laangaab' is a Somali slur for minority/short-lineage clans used here to mock 'Ciisho' — insulting someone's clan status as inferior while tagging Abgaal/Hawiye clan hashtags.

Post labels a Rwandan Hutu user as a 'genocidaire' still planning to kill, using ethnic slur 'muhutu' — while ostensibly condemning Hutu extremism, the framing collectively attributes genocidal intent to all Hutus and uses dangerous-speech existential-threat framing.
'Gaal raac' (follower of infidels/apostate-traitor) is a religious-nationalist slur used to denounce a named individual as a traitor to the Somali homeland.

Post praises a Somali critic of the Federal Government, calling Somalia a 'failed genocidal entity' and complaining about double standards on Israel relations — political/geopolitical polemic against the Somali state rather than targeted ethnic hate speech.

The post disputes historical claims about Isaaq clan dominance, accusing an interlocutor of fabricating ethnic/clan identity by mislabelling Oromos as Isaaq — this is a counter-argument in a clan-history dispute rather than a direct hate-speech attack.
A political allegation attributing Mungiki militia violence to a named politician (Gachagua), citing a third party — political accusation against an individual rather than group hate speech.

The post frames the Mt Kenya ethnic community as a targeted group being systematically eliminated through alcohol and money (accusation of a conspiratorial genocide), invoking an existential-threat narrative and an accusation-mirror dynamic characteristic of dangerous speech.

A political timeline attacking President Ruto's record with insults ('murderer', 'thief'), directed at a specific named political individual rather than an identity group — political criticism with abusive language.
A mocking personal profile of a named individual ('Mzee Waruthu') focusing on alleged corruption and low education — individual-targeted mockery rather than group hate speech.
Criticism of Kenyan political history (Anglo leasing, Kibaki era), labelling a political network 'criminal' — political critique without identity-group targeting.

The post publicly accuses and tags a specific individual (@Yaska21geesi) of funding militia attacks on Laascanood in 2023, calling on others to 'dig into' their account — a targeted harassment/reputational attack on a named person that could incite pile-on abuse.

Describes an armed group affiliated with the Sudanese Armed Forces as a terrorist organisation committing atrocities — conflict-reporting/commentary framing rather than incitement against a civilian identity group, though 'jihadi Islamist' carries derogatory religious labelling.

Alleges that Iran, Turkey and Qatar back the Sudanese junta through Muslim Brotherhood military ties — political/geopolitical commentary with anti-Islamist framing but no direct incitement against a civilian group.

The post dehumanises Omani-origin families in Mombasa as 'in-bred degenerates' causing economic harm, calls for severing ties with them — combining ethnic/national dehumanisation with an exclusion demand and implicit incitement against a specific community.

The post stereotypes Kenyan police as 'useless' and accuses them collectively of child rape in Haiti — a national-group insult and serious unsubstantiated collective accusation against Kenyans deployed abroad.
Complaint about foreign workers replacing Kenyan workers who demand higher wages — economic grievance framing with mild anti-foreigner sentiment but no explicit dehumanisation or incitement.
A rhetorical political rant about land and wealth inequality framed as a counter to perceived naivety — populist political grievance without targeting an identity group with slurs or dehumanisation.

'Kasongo' is a dismissive/slang reference to Congolese nationals ('wapewe citizen wakae huko' = 'give them citizenship and let them stay there'), suggesting foreign nationals be sent away — mild xenophobic dismissal.

Anti-colonial rhetorical post lamenting cultural assimilation and framing non-indigenous Kenyans as 'aliens' — expresses political/anti-colonial grievance with 'aliens' carrying mild othering but no direct incitement.

Directed at Qatar's foreign ministry, the post labels Qatar a 'home of terrorists' and accuses it of funding terrorists — political/national-foreigner insult against a state and its population rather than a civilian identity group.
Targets US Congresswoman Ilhan Omar (Somali-born) with demands to 'send her back' to Somalia — xenophobic incitement calling for forced deportation of a named individual on ethnic/national grounds.

Uses 'Faqash' (Barre-regime slur) to mock and dismiss the target, then issues an exclusion demand — explicitly stating the person will 'never set foot in Somaliland' — constituting implicit incitement to expulsion.

Conflates Somalis/Muslims with Al-Shabaab terrorists, calls for revival of Mungiki (a violent Kikuyu militia) and Mau Mau to 'defend' land, uses 'kihii' (uncircumcised ethnic slur against non-Kikuyu), framing Somalis as an existential threat to be expelled from Nairobi.
'Kihii' is a derogatory Kikuyu-origin slur meaning 'uncircumcised boy', used here as a general ethnic insult directed at the target.

Equates Somalis/Muslims with Al-Shabaab, calls for Mungiki and Mau Mau militia mobilisation to exclude them from Kenya, framing Somalis as an existential alien threat incompatible with Kenyan citizenship.
Explicitly calls on Kikuyu to revive Mungiki and Mau Mau militia groups to 'defend' against Somalis labelled collectively as 'ALSHABABs', demanding their territorial exclusion from Kenya.
Uses 'mungiki' (violent Kikuyu criminal gang) as a derogatory label for a president and their supporters, attacking Kikuyu ethnic identity through militia association.

Post criticises Kikuyu and Kalenjin ethnic groups ('kikuyus/kales') for allegedly monopolising national resources in Nairobi at the expense of others — ethnic-political grievance framed as group blame.

'Malaya' (prostitute) attacks a woman's dignity; 'kihii' is an ethnic slur; the phrase 'lazima amuue' ('he must kill her') constitutes an explicit threat of lethal violence against a woman, while 'KARMA' functions as a veiled threat.

Post implies that foreigners (Ugandans/Somalis implied by Mombasa Road/Parklands land context) were allowed into Kenya through corrupt Moi-era border policies, othering them as illegitimate land occupants.
Post is a factual/historical dispute about island geography and colonial land transactions near the Horn of Africa — no hate speech or identity-based attack present.

Post falsely and approvingly claims KDF troops killed '1 million Somalis' during operations in Somalia, presenting mass killing of an ethnic group as a boast rather than a war crime — glorifying ethnic mass killing.

Labels a Somali woman a 'terrorist', collective-blames 'Somalis' for a tribal war, then states retaliation against Somalis is 'justifiable' — constituting incitement to ethnic group violence under the Rabat threshold framing.

Post calls out government neglect of Mwingi security and collectively labels armed Somali pastoralists 'Somali Terrorists', conflating an ethnic community with terrorism while directing political criticism at authorities.

'Nywele ngumu' (racial slur for Black Africans) is used self-referentially, but the post frames Somalis in Eastleigh as a parasitic 'monster' consuming Kenyan/African wealth and subverting politics — an existential threat trope targeting Somalis as foreigners.

Post condemns both the killing of Kamba civilians by Somali pastoralists AND retaliatory mob violence against Garissa-bound buses, calling for justice rather than inciting further violence — this is counter-speech/condemnation, not hate speech.

Written in Kamba, the post appeals to a politician to visit Mwingi during community distress and refers to 'Somali camel herders' as aggressors in a 'heavy attack', using a dismissive ethnic-occupational label to frame Somalis collectively as attackers.

Post is political mobilisation rhetoric against President Ruto, calling for a nationwide anti-government revolution by 2027 — political criticism of an individual leader without ethnic or identity-group targeting.

A TASIS (Sudan) propaganda post framing Tigrayan fighters as pawns of 'terrorist Muslim Brotherhood', using religious-political othering to delegitimise an ethnic group's involvement — accusation-mirror framing linking an ethnic group to an existential religious threat, but directed at Sudan/Ethiopia actors with peripheral South Sudan relevance.

The post makes a political correction about TPLF access to Sudan, then uses 'langab' (a Somali slur for low-lineage/minority person) combined with 'Ogaden' as a clan-based insult to demean the interlocutor.
The post stereotypes Somalis in Kenya as passport fraudsters, using collective accusation to frame an ethnic/national group as criminals abusing the Kenyan system.

The post criticises the Kenyan president for allegedly giving IDs to 'aliens' and 'foreigners', framing migrants as an electoral manipulation tool — primarily political criticism with nativist undertones but no explicit group slur or incitement.

The post — apparently about a Kenyan national placed in the US context ('OUR HOME', 'OUR COUNTRY HISTORY') — expresses nativist outrage at a foreigner's presence and demands accountability, without a specific identity-group slur; context is too ambiguous to confirm East Africa relevance.

terms: want you out of our country
exp: The post explicitly calls for expulsion of a person (implied to be Somali or foreign-origin) from Kenya on grounds of not speaking national languages, constituting a direct exclusion/removal demand directed at an individual perceived as a foreigner.

The Swahili post dismisses concern about a Luhya person becoming president by questioning what any ruling tribe has done for ordinary citizens — primarily tribal political critique with a crude insult ('inaskuashia nini kwa mkundu') rather than organised hatred or incitement.
The post quotes a Swahili welcome song ('Wageni, mwakaribishwa' — 'Guests, you are welcome, our Kenya, no worries'), expressing a positive, inclusive sentiment with no hateful content.

The Swahili post reports that the Kamba community ('Wakamba') have decided to shut down following inter-communal attacks — this reads as descriptive reporting of ethnic tension rather than itself constituting hate speech, though the framing is ambiguous.

The post calls Hawiye clan members 'impure/filth' (najaas), 'thieves', 'their sheikhs', labels them as psychologically sick (cuqdad=grudge/resentment), and calls for separating the best from them and seizing a mosque by force, constituting dehumanisation and an incitement to exclusion/expulsion.

Swahili post criticising a political figure for allegedly using religion to divide ('MAVI'=shit, 'KIFALA'=possibly 'fool/idiot' slang) and calling for political mobilisation on 9 December; primarily political criticism with mild insult rather than identity-group hate.

Somali-language news-style report alleging an unlawful (sharcidarro) kidnapping of a peacekeeper by Villa Somalia-linked terrorist/extremist elements (qawleysatada argagixisada); reporting/condemnation of alleged state abuse, not hate speech.
Post uses 'tuug/tuugnimo' (thief/thievery) as a generalising slur applied to Somalis as a collective, stereotyping an entire national/ethnic group as inherently criminal.
Directed at a specific user, using 'xaarood' — a derogatory slur targeting the Darod clan (xaar=faeces + Darod) — combined with a scatological insult, constituting targeted clan-based harassment.

Post makes sweeping derogatory generalisations about Dinka political power as illegitimate and purchased, and predicts their irrelevance; sits on the border between political criticism and ethnic disparagement but contains no slurs or incitement.

Post collectively attributes child abduction, parental killings, and ritual body-marking to the entire Murle ethnic community as cultural practice, constituting a dehumanising collective accusation that mirrors atrocity framing and could reinforce retaliatory violence narratives.

Somali post asserting Darod clan territorial claims over Mogadishu and dismissing Hawiye authority there, invoking clan-political rivalry with reference to President Muse; primarily political-territorial clan dispute rather than dehumanising hate speech.

Post calls Somali-unionist (non-Somaliland) Isaaq opponents 'faqash orphans' (Barre-regime filth), labels them 'xaarood xaaraan' (Darod-slur + forbidden/cursed) 'devil worshippers', and invokes the death of dictator Siad Barre as a warning threat to opponents of Somaliland sovereignty.
Post uses 'camjiec' — an anti-Nuer ethnic slur in South Sudanese context — combined with 'thiele wec' (possibly 'stupid/mad cattle') to demean a person identified as Nuer.

Post uses 'Jareer Bantus' — a racial-ethnic slur for Somali Bantu communities — while superficially praising them alongside Hawiye as loyal, but framing all other clans as idol-worshippers; the slur term itself constitutes identity-based insult even in a nominally positive context.

Policy-reform commentary criticising Somalia's 4.5 clan power-sharing formula as a 'political cancer' suppressing meritocracy; political critique of a governance system without targeting any identity group with hate speech.

Reporting an official accusation that President Hassan Sheikh is an apostate (murtad/ex-Muslim) — a charge that in the Somali context carries implicit capital-punishment connotations and constitutes a dangerous existential framing against an individual.

Post uses 'Hutuwiye' (derogatory portmanteau of Hutu+Hawiye) and 'Adoogaas' (monkey-adjacent slur for Isaaq/Somaliland speakers) while mockingly calling Karanle sub-clan members 'Oromo' to delegitimise their Somali identity, and 'Nacala' (curse on them).

Post directed at a Somali user uses 'jareer' (racial slur for Bantu/hard-hair people) to mock and demean, alongside stereotypes about child marriage and khat, while contrasting them unfavourably with 'nation-builders'.

Post combines the racial slur 'jareer' with 'baboons' to dehumanise Somali Bantu people while claiming only Somaliland Isaaq are 'original Somalis', constituting both ethnic dehumanisation and exclusion of Bantu Somalis from national identity.
Post uses 'Adoogaas' (monkey-derived slur) to mock Isaaq dialect, dismissing their Somali speech as corrupted while counter-accusing them of provocation.

Post mocks a Somali interlocutor by noting they must travel to 'Jareer Bantu countries' (racial slur for sub-Saharan African nations) to experience a functioning state, using the slur to demean both the target and African countries simultaneously.

Post uses 'midgaan' — a deeply derogatory slur for the Madhiban/Gabooye caste — to impute sexual predation, then dehumanises Hawiye ('Hutuwiye') and Darod ('daroogo') as 'creatures', targeting both caste and clan identities.

Post uses 'jareer' to racially demean AMISOM troops from Kenya/Uganda/Burundi, frames them as sexually exploiting Somali women as an accusation-mirror shaming tactic, and uses dehumanising 'these people' language to deny their humanity.

Post uses 'Jareer' (racial slur for Bantu Africans) and 'Bomalians' (derogatory blend for certain Somalis) to mock Somalis for allegedly siding with African AMISOM troops over Arab allies, framing it as racial disloyalty.

Post uses 'Jareerweyne' as a self-identifying clan/community name in an apparently affirmative geographic-demographic context; no hate speech detected — this appears to be community self-identification rather than a slur.

Post calls Hawiye supporters 'Hutuwiye/hutus' (genocidal derogatory portmanteau) and 'slaves of Ugandese', mocking a Somali political initiative as a 'scam' and gloating over its failure with ethnic taunts.

Post praises Isaaq as noble patriots while blaming the 'Hutuwiye' (Hawiye slur) and 'daroogo-Jeberti confederation' (Darod+Jeberti slur compound) for destroying Somalia, using 'Zoomalia' (zoo+Somalia derogatory) to mock the remaining Somali state.

Post uses 'Iidoor' (anti-Isaaq slur, variant of idoor/inader) while labelling the SNM (Somaliland founding movement) as terrorists and criminals, framing Somaliland's existence as illegal and invoking Somali territorial integrity.
